newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Mladic created army in Serb warrior tradition.
newsitem.headline: Mladic created army in Serb warrior tradition.

text.p: General Ratko Mladic, reported on Thursday to have resigned after a power struggle with his political masters, fashioned the Bosnia Serb Army (BSA) in his own image.
In the years when the fighting in Bosnia ran in the BSA's favour, it was a model of ruthlessness, daring and brutality in the Serb warrior tradition.
Even in decline, it was capable of acts of breathtaking audacity, such as the blitz on Srebrenica or the use of hostage U.N. peacekeepers as human shields against NATO air attacks.
Everything the BSA did in battle bore the imprint of its 52-year-old creator, commander and arch-strategist.
It earned him a soubriquet as the "Butcher of Bosnia" and two U.N. indictments for war crimes in the process.

The independent Yugoslav VIP news agency said on Thursday Mladic had written to the civilian leadership in the Bosnian Serb capital Pale to confirm he had handed authority to his deputy, General Manojlo Milovanovic.

VIP said one of Milovanovic's first tasks would be to attend a ceremony on Thursday in Pale where he would transfer his hours-old command to General Pero Colic, who has the support of the civilian leadership.
The move ended a battle for control of the BSA which flared earlier this month when Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic ordered the retirement of Mladic and most of his senior commanders.

Mladic's dismissal, along with most of his generals, by Plavsic was probably the surest sign since the Bosnian peace agreement a year ago that the political leadership had ruled out further war as a means of achieving its goals.
In the macho, hard-drinking world of the Bosnian Serb military, the war command's humiliation was undoubtedly compounded by the fact that they were purged by a woman.
The son of a World War Two partisan fighter killed in 1945, Mladic was a star officer in the old communist Yugoslav Federal Army (JNA) when Yugoslavia's disintegration began in 1991.
He won his first media fame in Knin in southern Croatia where his intervention ensured the success of a local Serb rebellion against Croatian rule.
When Bosnian Serbs rose in 1992 against Bosnia's Moslem-led secession, Mladic was hand-picked to command the new Bosnian Serb Army that swiftly overran 70 percent of the country.
The strategy Mladic employed formed the basis of the indictments laid against him by the U.N. war crimes tribunal.
The key element was ethnic cleansing to drive Bosnian Moslems and Croats from their homes in territory claimed for the embryonic Bosnian Serb Republic.

The BSA used its tank and artillery superiority to lay sieges against Moslem towns in east and central Bosnia and the capital Sarajevo that became a byword for civilian slaughter not seen in Europe for half a century.
The 22,000 troops of the U.N. Protection Force (UNPROFOR), crippled by political and diplomatic constraints, stood by more or less helplessly as Mladic's army carved up Bosnia.
The strategy culminated in the horror of Srebrenica, a United Nations safe area for Moslems in east Bosnia which the BSA captured in July 1995 under Mladic's personal command.
Some 8,000 Moslem men disappeared in BSA custody after surrendering. Many were believed to have been executed in a four-day bloodbath by firing squads and bulldozed into mass graves.
It was almost Mladic's last fling in a war with which his political backers in Serbia as well as the international community had lost patience.
The BSA was crumbling, suffering defeats from Moslem and Croat forces elsewhere in Bosnia and its ability to fight hit by the withdrawal of equipment and fuel supplies from Serbia.
Mladic, a political player in his own right and notoriously impatient of civilian authority, became an albatross for the Bosnian Serb leadership which tried unsuccessfully to sack him in 1995.
He remains a hero for ordinary Bosnian Serbs and commanded the professional respect of United Nations and NATO officers who dealt with him.
Diplomats believe Mladic shaped the Bosnia conflict more than almost any other individual until Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic reasserted his authority last year and insisted on peace.
